notes.meaning: Mary Magdalene arrives at the garden tomb early Sunday morning while it is still dark. She finds the large stone rolled back and the entrance wide open. Her heart sinks because she assumes someone has disturbed the resting place of Jesus.
Mary runs immediately to Peter and John to report what she found. She fears that enemies or grave robbers have carried the Lord's body away. She does not yet realize that Jesus has conquered death.

Peter and John set out at once toward the tomb after hearing Mary's troubling news. They want to see the condition of the grave with their own eyes. Their prompt departure shows their deep love and urgent concern for Jesus.

The two disciples run side by side, but John runs faster and reaches the tomb ahead of Peter. Being younger and lighter on his feet, John arrives first at the site. Their race reflects their intense eagerness to learn the truth.
John stoops down to look through the low entrance of the tomb. He sees the linen burial cloths lying on the stone bench inside. Out of reverence or hesitation, he pauses and does not step inside.

Simon Peter arrives right behind John and boldly walks straight into the tomb. He carefully inspects the burial wrappings left lying on the bench. Peter's bold nature leads him to examine the evidence up close.

Peter notices that the cloth used to wrap Jesus' head is neatly rolled up in a spot separate from the other linens. Grave robbers would never take the time to unwrap a corpse and fold the wrappings so neatly. The peaceful, orderly scene proves that Christ left the tomb calmly by His own power.

John now enters the tomb as well, encouraged by Peter's lead. He observes the orderly placement of the empty grave clothes and immediately believes that Jesus has risen. Seeing the calm scene convinces him before he even sees the Lord.

Up to this moment, the disciples had not truly grasped what the Old Testament Scriptures taught about the Messiah rising from the dead. Jesus had warned them of His death and resurrection, but grief had clouded their minds. Now God's truth is beginning to break through their confusion.

Having inspected the empty tomb, Peter and John head back to their lodgings in Jerusalem. They leave the garden full of deep wonder and mixed thoughts about what has taken place. There was nothing more for them to do at the open grave.

Mary returns to the tomb and lingers outside alone, weeping bitter tears. Her heart is broken because she still believes her Master's body has been stolen. As she weeps, she bends down once more to look inside the cave.

Mary sees two angels dressed in bright white garments sitting inside the tomb. One sits where Jesus' head had rested and the other where His feet had lain. Their presence frames the empty place with heavenly glory.

The angels gently ask Mary why she is weeping, hinting that grief is out of place on this victorious morning. Mary replies that someone has taken her Lord away and she does not know where to find Him. Her intense personal love for Jesus completely fills her thoughts.

After answering the angels, Mary turns around and sees a man standing nearby. It is Jesus Himself, but she fails to recognize Him. Her tear-filled eyes and heavy sorrow keep her from seeing that her living Lord is right beside her.

Jesus asks Mary why she is crying and whom she is looking for, gently prompting her to think beyond her grief. Assuming He is the caretaker of the garden, she asks Him where the body was taken so she can go and carry it away herself. Her loving devotion makes her willing to shoulder any burden for her Lord.

Jesus speaks her personal name, Mary, in His familiar and tender voice. The single word opens her eyes, and she turns to Him in sudden, joyful recognition. She cries out Rabboni, an Aramaic title of deep honor meaning my Teacher.

Mary joyfully grasps Jesus, but He tells her not to cling to Him as if to keep Him in the old earthly way. He explains that He has not yet ascended to heaven, meaning there is still time before His final departure. Instead, He sends her on an urgent mission to tell His disciples that He is returning to His Father and theirs.

Mary Magdalene obeys at once and hurries to the disciples with the glorious news that she has seen the Lord. She faithfully repeats every word Jesus spoke to her. God honors this devoted woman by making her the very first witness of the resurrection.

On Sunday evening, the disciples gather behind locked doors because they are afraid the Jewish leaders will arrest them next. Suddenly Jesus appears and stands right among them without opening the locked doors. He greets them with peace, replacing their terror with heavenly comfort.

Jesus shows them the wound marks in His hands and His pierced side. These physical marks prove beyond all doubt that He is not a ghost, but their truly risen Master in a real body. Overjoyed and relieved, the disciples rejoice to see their living Lord.

Jesus repeats His greeting of peace to calm their hearts and prepare them for a great assignment. Just as the Father sent Jesus into the world to reveal God's love, Jesus now commissions His followers to go into the world as His ambassadors. They are to carry His message of salvation to everyone.

Jesus breathes on the disciples and tells them to receive the Holy Spirit. This action recalls God breathing life into the first man at creation, pointing to the spiritual new creation Christ brings. It serves as a foretaste and promise of the full power of the Spirit that would arrive at Pentecost.

differ.view: In official Lutheran teaching, Jesus breathes the Spirit on His followers to give the church what is called the "Office of the Keys"—the authority from Christ to announce God’s forgiveness (absolution) to those who turn from sin, and to withhold it from those who do not repent. Pastors carry out this duty publicly on behalf of the whole congregation.

Scholars in this tradition read Jesus breathing on the disciples as the moment they were indwelt by the Holy Spirit and given new spiritual life (regeneration, or being born again), just like God breathed life into Adam in Genesis. They view this quiet gift of eternal life on Easter as distinct from Pentecost in Acts 2, where the Spirit came with power to equip them for public preaching.

notes.meaning: Jesus gives the disciples authority to announce God's forgiveness of sins to all who repent and believe in Christ. They also carry the authority to declare that those who reject the gospel remain under God's judgment. The apostles do not forgive sins by their own power, but authoritatively proclaim God's terms of pardon.

differ.view: Lutherans teach that Christ gave the church the "Office of the Keys," which is the special power to give or withhold forgiveness. When a pastor speaks absolution (declaring that God forgives a person) to someone who repents (turns away from sin), that word is just as real and certain in heaven as if Jesus spoke it Himself.

Presbyterians understand this verse as the "keys of the kingdom," which church leaders exercise through preaching and church discipline (the work of guiding members and addressing unrepentant sin). Church leaders do not forgive sins by their own power, but they faithfully declare God's pardon to those who trust in Christ and remove unrepentant people from the church fellowship.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics teach that Jesus gave the apostles and their ordained successors actual authority to forgive or retain sins, which requires the faithful to confess their specific sins aloud to a priest in the sacrament of reconciliation.

notes.meaning: Thomas, whose Greek name Didymus means the twin, was absent when Jesus first appeared to the disciples. By missing that gathering, he missed the comfort and proof his fellow disciples received. His absence left him trapped in deep sorrow and loneliness.

The other disciples joyfully tell Thomas that they have seen the risen Lord. Thomas stubbornly refuses to take their word for it, demanding to see the nail wounds and put his hand into Jesus' pierced side. His grief makes him demand exact physical proof before he will believe.

A week later, on the next Sunday, the disciples gather inside again, and this time Thomas is with them. Even though the doors are locked, Jesus appears in their midst just as before. He greets them once more with His reassuring words of peace.

Jesus turns directly to Thomas and invites him to touch His hands and place his hand into His wounded side. By repeating Thomas's exact demands, Jesus shows that He knew every word spoken in secret. He tenderly urges Thomas to stop doubting and step into living faith.

Overcome with awe, Thomas cries out to Jesus, calling Him my Lord and my God. He does not merely express surprise; he openly confesses that the risen Jesus is the true God. This is the highest confession of Christ's divine nature in the entire Gospel.

Jesus accepts Thomas's faith because he saw the physical proof, but He declares a special blessing on future believers who will trust without seeing. True faith relies on the trustworthy word of God rather than physical sight. All who believe the apostles' testimony share in this promised blessing.

Jesus performed countless other miraculous signs in the presence of His disciples that are not recorded in this book. John chose a select number of miracles that clearly revealed who Jesus is. No single book could ever contain the full greatness of Christ's work.

John explains that he recorded these specific signs so that readers would believe that Jesus is the Christ, the promised Savior and Son of God. True faith in Jesus brings spiritual life now and eternal life forever. Trusting in His name is the only path to real and lasting life.
